Des pâtes farcies, une nouvelle sauce Tomate Mozzarella fondante et un gratin doré à souhait… Qui peut résister ? @viviana_pisacane et Monelle @not_so_superflu nous proposent des Conchiglie Rigate avec la Sauce Tomate & Mozzarella @barilla_fr pour une recette végétarienne ultra-gourmande 🇮🇹❤️. Le plat qui met tout le monde d’accord, petits et grands ! Ingrédients pour 2 à 3 personnes 280 g de conchiglie rigate Collezione Barilla 1 pot de Sauce Tomate & Mozzarella Barilla 650 g de brocoli (fleurettes et tiges tendres) 350 g de parmesan râpé 2 gousses d’ail 35 g d’amandes effilées 35 ml d’huile d’olive vierge Sel, poivre 50 à 100 ml d’eau de cuisson des brocolis Préparation Coupez le brocoli et faites cuire les fleurettes dans l’eau bouillante salée jusqu’à ce qu’il soit tendre. Réservez un peu d’eau de cuisson, puis égouttez. Faites revenir doucement l’ail émincé dans 25 ml d’huile d’olive. Ajoutez le brocoli et faites sauter quelques minutes. Mixez les ¾ du brocoli avec l’ail et l’huile restante et un peu d’eau de cuisson pour obtenir une crème épaisse. Ajoutez le reste du brocoli haché. Salez, poivrez. Précuisez les conchiglie 2 à 3 min de moins que le temps indiqué, puis égouttez. Versez la moitié de la sauce Barilla dans un plat à gratin. Farcissez les conchiglie de crème de brocoli à l’aide d’une poche à douille. Disposez-les dans le plat, ajoutez le reste de sauce et parsemez de parmesan. Enfournez 15 à 20 min à 190 °C, jusqu’à ce que les pâtes soient cuites et gratinées. Couvrez si besoin. Faites toaster les amandes à sec dans une poêle, puis parsemez-les sur les pâtes à la sortie du four. Servez dans des assiettes creuses. Note : aucune crème ni aucun fromage dans la farce. Den Knoblauch dazu pressen und kurz mitbraten. Die roten Linsen (vorher kurz abspülen) und die Kichererbsen in die Pfanne geben. Mit Paprikapulver würzen und alles gut vermengen. Die stückigen Tomaten hinzufügen und mit Wasser oder Brühe aufgießen. Bei mittlerer Hitze ca. 20–25 Minuten köcheln lassen, bis die Linsen weich und cremig sind. Mit Salz und Pfeffer abschmecken. Während die Linsen köcheln, den Kern-Mix zusammen mit den Thymianblättchen in einer Pfanne rösten, bis die Kerne goldbraun sind, Olivenöl dazu geben und ein paar Minuten aromatisch ziehen lassen. Die Linsen in eine Schüssel geben. Einen großen Klecks veganen Joghurt darauf platzieren. Den warmen Thymian-Crunch darüber geben, mit frischer Minze bestreuen und mit ordentlich Zitronensaft abrunden. Adrienne's Classic Desserts provides an assortment of healthier sweets that everyone can enjoy.  Try these delicious Vegan Caramel Chocolate Chip Cookies.  They are made with decadent, non-dairy caramel chocolate chips, coconut sugar, vegan butter and some other key ingredients.  For more delicious recipes, follow on Instagram @adriennesclassicdesserts.  If you would like to subscribe to my newsletter for other recipes, tap the linktree in my bio. Vegan Carmel Chocolate Chip Cookies Ingredients: 1/2 Cup of vegan butter, softened slightly 1 Cup of coconut sugar 3 Tablespoons of organic sugar 1/4 Cup of unsweetened almond milk 2 Teaspoons of vanilla extract 1 3/4 Cups of all-purpose gluten free flour 1 Teaspoon of baking soda 1/2 Teaspoon of Himalayan salt 1 Cup of vegan Carmel nondairy chocolate chips Directions: -Add the vegan butter, coconut sugar and granulated sugar to a large bowl. Then use a handheld mixer then cream the butter and coconut sugar until combined about 2 minutes. Add the plant based milk and vanilla extract then combine ingredient’s. -Add the gluten-free all purpose flour, baking soda and Himalayan salt to the bowl. Fold in that nondairy chocolate chips. -Cover the cookie dough with plastic wrap and place in the refrigerator to chill for at least 30 minutes or overnight. -Preheat the oven to 350F degrees and line a baking sheet with parchment paper. Use a cookie scooper and place the dough into balls and transfer to a baking sheet. Bake the cookies for 11 - 15 minutes on the middle rack of the oven. Remove the cookies form the oven then cool for 5 minutes on the baking sheet. Enjoy! #veganrecipes #healthyeating #desserts #cleaneating #healthydesserts #vegandesserts #cookies 0:00 / 0:37 ​

I love lions mane mushrooms! Here’s a socca pizza I created with these mushrooms and an orange curry sauce. Soccas are a type of flatbread. I make mine with chickpea or breadfruit flour. I’m using my new toy, a carbon steel griddle. For the socca batter: roasted red onion, garlic, sweet peppers, chickpea flour, nutritional yeast, a little avocado oil, herbs and spices, and unsweetened coconut milk. For the orange curry sauce: fresh orange juice, ginger-turmeric paste, sambal, monkfruit sweetener, and oat yogurt. Marinate the lions mane mushrooms in the orange curry sauce and set aside for at least an hour. We’re ready to cook! Preheat your griddle, add a bit of avocado oil, and pour some of the socca batter onto the griddle. Cook one side until little air pockets form, then flip them until done. Let’s bake our socca pizza! Add wilted spinach, tomatoes, walnut cheese, and the orange curry sauce. Now, into the oven it goes! While the socca is baking, grill the mushrooms while basting with the orange curry sauce. Once the socca pizza is baked, add the grilled mushrooms and you are ready to eat! Vitamins become increasingly important as we age because the body’s ability to absorb and utilize nutrients from food naturally declines. Azerbaijan now welcomes you by rail, with Azerbaijan Railways offering a comfortable and scenic way to explore a land of striking contrasts and living culture. In Baku, history and modern design exist in a constant dialogue. The flowing architecture of the Heydar Aliyev Centre stands in contrast to the timeless streets of Icherisheher, creating a city where past and present shape one another. As evening arrives, Baku shifts into a vibrant nightlife scene, filled with concerts, festivals, rooftop spaces, and music that carries through the night. Further along the route, Ganja reveals a more historic and soulful character. Known for its architectural heritage, spiritual landmarks like the Imamzadeh Mausoleum, and the legacy of poet Nizami Ganjavi, the city reflects centuries of cultural depth. Its cuisine adds another layer, with traditional flavours such as Ganja dovga, vegetarian grape leaf dolma with rice, and pakhlava offering a true taste of local heritage. I almost looked past the woman who saved my husband's life. She was seventy-nine, sitting alone at the booth next to ours at the Cracker Barrel off Highway 31. A glass of milk in front of her. She kept stirring it. She wasn't eating. If I'd known, the night I leaned over and asked her to join us, that she was the only reason my husband would still be walking into his workshop at sixty-seven — I would have asked her to stay a little longer. Looked at her a little harder. Taken a breath. But I didn't know. I just slid over and pulled out the chair across from Earl and waved her toward us. Her name is Joyce. She's seventy-nine now. She was a hospice nurse for thirty-one years before she retired. She still asks before she pours herself coffee from our pot. She says "ma'am" to the waitress at Cracker Barrel every Tuesday evening. She started joining Earl and me for Tuesday lunches the second month after we met. She started calling me "honey" the third. Her husband had been dead eight months by the time I met her. Earl and I had been having Tuesday dinner at Cracker Barrel for fourteen years. After every quarterly nephrology appointment, we'd drive there straight from the lab. We'd sit across from each other and not talk about the numbers. We'd just order the same thing and look at the salt shaker. That Tuesday in March, I had watched the elderly woman at the next table for almost a full minute. She wasn't eating. She was stirring a glass of milk with a spoon, very slowly, the way someone stirs when they have nowhere to be and no one to be with. I'd seen her in there before. I almost said nothing. I leaned over anyway. I'm going to tell you why I asked, because the answer matters. It's not because I was being noble. I'd like to say I was. I wasn't. Earl and I had been married thirty-eight years. The last fourteen months had been the quietest of them. He'd come home from the workshop earlier and earlier until he just stopped going. By Tuesday nights at Cracker Barrel he'd order, eat half his plate, and stare past me toward the rocking chairs by the front door. Some quiet takes longer than you expect to do anything with. I was sixty-four by then. Earl was sixty-seven. I knew something was sliding away from us and I didn't know what to do about it. I had a hole in my chest the size of my husband. Joyce had a hole in hers the size of the man who had died beside her last spring. That was the whole reason. We needed each other. That's all. Joyce asked me what I did for a living. I told her I'd taught fourth grade for thirty-six years before I retired. Her eyes flickered. "Do you miss them?" she asked. I told her some Tuesdays more than others. Mostly I missed having a room full of people who needed something from me. "What about your husband? What does he do?" I told her Earl had been an electrician forty-two years. Still kept a workshop in the garage. Rebuilt vintage tube radios on weekends, or used to. She nodded. The way she nodded was the way a nurse nods when she's filing information away to look at later. "My Walter rebuilt radios too. Amateur radio operator for fifty years. He died last May." She set her spoon down. There was a small spiral notebook on the table next to her purse. The kind a nurse carries in her uniform pocket. It was worn at the corners. There were three pens clipped to the spiral. The inside back cover had folded papers tucked into it — lab printouts, I'd find out later. Walter's. I didn't know it then, but that notebook had thirty-one years of hospice notes in it. The last six months of pages were about Walter. Earl shook her hand at the end of dinner. He doesn't usually do that with strangers. He told her if she ever wanted company on a Tuesday, we ate there every week at six. She came the next Tuesday. And the Tuesday after that. The first three months weren't easy for her. I won't tell you they were because that wouldn't be true. She'd ask about her purse twice during each meal. She kept it on her lap the whole time, like she might have to leave. She drank water instead of coffee for the first six weeks because she said caffeine made her remember things she was trying not to remember. She didn't open up about Walter until July. July was when Earl asked her what kind of radios Walter had built and she pulled a photograph out of her wallet — Walter sitting at a workbench covered in vacuum tubes, headphones around his neck. Something about Earl knowing what every component in the picture was — something about a man who recognized the work of another man's hands — broke through. She started joining us at our house for Tuesday dinner two weeks after that conversation. She started calling me "honey" the night I served pot roast. She said "Honey, this is the first pot roast I've had since Walter died" and I almost dropped the gravy boat on the floor. By October she was bringing me a small mason jar of preserves every Tuesday. She'd set it on the kitchen counter without saying anything. Just put it there and walk past. That was the kind of friend she was. Earl is sixty-seven years old. He's been an electrician since he was twenty-five. Forty-two years with a wire stripper in his hand. He owned a small contracting outfit with his name on the truck — Whitaker Electric — until he retired at sixty-three. His longest-tenured apprentice was a man named Curtis who'd been with him for twenty-four years. Earl wired every receptacle in our house. He wired the bell system at First Methodist. He rebuilt a 1962 Zenith console for our granddaughter's wedding present last year. He's also been on a blood pressure medication called lisinopril for twelve years, and a second one called amlodipine for the last six. He's been on metformin for eight. His body is not cooperating the same way anymore. The fatigue doesn't lift. By seven in the evening his ankles are so swollen he can't get his work boots off without help. His energy is gone. He falls asleep in his recliner some afternoons after lunch. I quietly turn the television down and let him sleep. Twice in the last six months he's gotten up from the dinner table three times to go to the bathroom. Once he mentioned the foam in the toilet before bed and I didn't know what to say. He never brought it up again. He's stopped going out to the workshop. The 1958 Philco he was rebuilding for our grandson has been sitting on the bench under a cloth for fourteen months. Curtis came by once to check on him and I watched Earl pretend the radio was almost finished. It wasn't. He couldn't read the schematic anymore. I know. Ten months into our Tuesday lunches with Joyce, Earl came back from his quarterly nephrology appointment and didn't speak for three hours. That night he told me he was going to put the workshop tools up on Facebook Marketplace. His doctor was a man named Dr. Patel who had known Earl for six years and called him "Mr. Whitaker." Dr. Patel had told him his eGFR was 48. Stage 3a. They'd check again in three months. I asked if there was anything we could do. Dr. Patel said "diet, exercise, blood pressure control — you're already doing all of it." Then he asked if Earl had talked to anyone about depression. He said the energy issues sometimes had a mental health component at this stage. Earl had nodded, shaken his hand, and driven home. He sat at our kitchen table and told me he'd wired half this county with his hands — and now his hands couldn't hold a schematic in focus long enough to read it. He didn't cry. Earl doesn't cry. He just looked at the salt shaker for a long time. Joyce was at our Tuesday lunch the next week when I broke down in the booth. I hadn't meant to. I'd been holding it. The waitress had set down our biscuits and I told Joyce about the antidepressant suggestion and my eyes filled before I could stop them. Joyce set down her coffee. "Honey. I have been waiting eight months for you to ask me what I've been seeing." She reached into her purse. Pulled out the spiral notebook. Tore out a page. Wrote three words on it in pencil. Slid it across the table. The page said: Hibiscus. Nephron oxidation. I read it twice. I put it in my purse. "I'll explain. But not here. Come to my apartment Thursday afternoon. Bring Earl if he'll come. Just promise me you'll listen all the way through before you tell me I'm crazy." "I promise." She finished her coffee like nothing had happened. That night I drove to Kroger. I stood in the tea aisle for ten minutes and found a box of Bigelow hibiscus — $4.99, red box, picture of flowers on the front. The woman had written hibiscus. It said hibiscus. I bought two boxes. I steeped a cup that night and another the next morning before Thursday arrived. Nothing. Earl drank his and said it tasted like watered-down cough syrup. I told him to keep trying. Thursday came. I drove. Earl sat in the passenger seat staring out the window the way he did at everything now. Joyce met us at the door of her apartment in a clean blouse. She had her spiral notebook under her arm. She hugged Earl for a long time before he sat down. He looked startled by it. He hugged her back. We had coffee. Joyce had a plate of shortbread out. Earl had three pieces and apologized. She told him to have more. Joyce sat down across from us. Folded her hands. Looked at Earl. "Mr. Whitaker. Margaret. I almost didn't bring this notebook out. I held it on my kitchen counter for forty minutes before you got here." "I'm a hospice nurse. I'm not a nephrologist. I might be wrong about all of this." Before she could go further I set the Bigelow box on the table. "Joyce. I bought this at Kroger Wednesday night. We've been steeping it. Nothing's happened." She looked at the box. Then she looked at me with an expression that was not quite a smile. "Margaret. That's not what I meant by hibiscus." She set the box to one side. "That's what almost everyone does first. I'm going to show you the difference." She took a breath. "But I'm going to start at the beginning. And I'm asking you to listen all the way to the end before you tell me whether I'm crazy. Because I think this matters." She opened the notebook. She didn't start with Earl. She started with Walter. "Mr. Whitaker. Margaret. I have to tell you about my husband. I don't talk about him because it still hurts and because I should have known better. But I've been carrying something for eight months and I should have told you sooner." She laid out the lab printouts first — the folded pages from the notebook's inside back cover. Her husband — Walter Hennessy — had been diagnosed with Stage 2 CKD at sixty-eight. eGFR 62. His nephrologist had told him to monitor it. Same words. Diet, exercise, blood pressure control. They'd check again in three months. Walter was a retired RCA technician. He'd worked on radar systems in Korea and tube televisions for thirty years after. He carved his initials into every chassis he ever rebuilt — WH, in the corner, where the customer would never see it. Joyce had taken care of dying patients for thirty-one years. She had not known what to do for her own husband. "I want to tell you who Walter was before I tell you what happened to him," Joyce said. "Because I need you to understand he was a man, not just a chart." Walter had built her a crystal radio for their first anniversary. It still sat on her dresser. She turned it on every night before bed. This was the first time I'd heard any of it. "Three months in, the fatigue started," Joyce said. She slid one of the printouts across the table. It was a follow-up note from Walter's first-year appointment. "Patient reports increased fatigue. Likely deconditioning. Counseled on activity." "Year two his ankles swelled. Doctor wrote: 'Mild edema, manage with elevation.' Year three he was up three times a night to pee. Year four he'd lost twelve pounds he hadn't been trying to lose. His wedding ring fell off in the sink one morning. He hadn't noticed." She pulled out another printout. "This is Walter's lab from month seven. eGFR 52. Doctor wrote 'trending in the right direction, manageable progression.'" She picked up another one. "Month eleven. eGFR 36. Doctor wrote 'progression consistent with stage, continue monitoring.'" Another one. "Month fourteen. eGFR 22. They started talking about a fistula. Three weeks later he was on dialysis. Six months after that he was gone." Joyce set the printout down. "The chart said his numbers were trending in the right direction the same month his kidneys started failing. The cuff said his pressure was fine. His A1C was fine. Everything the doctor was watching looked manageable." She looked at Earl. "Mr. Whitaker. You're on the same medications. Same eGFR Walter had eleven months before he started dialysis. Same symptoms now that he had then. Same thing your doctor is saying — that you're doing everything you can." She paused. "I lost my husband last May to this. I'm not losing the friend who knows what a 6SN7 tube does to the same thing if I can help it." She pulled out a thinner section of the notebook. Pages with words she'd looked up. Definitions in pencil in the margins. "I know how this is going to sound," she said. "I'm a retired hospice nurse telling you that two doctors with thirty years of practice between them are watching the wrong thing. I get how that sounds." "I read until I understood. I might still be wrong. If I am, tell me and I'll drop it. But please. Hear me out first." "The doctor has been watching the wrong thing the whole time. For Walter and for Earl." "Your eGFR is sliding because your nephrons are being damaged. That's it. That's the whole thing. The tiny filters in your kidneys are being attacked from the inside by toxic free radicals — and the filtration rate drops because there are fewer working nephrons left every month. Lisinopril controls pressure. Amlodipine relaxes the vessels. Metformin manages your blood sugar. They all manage a number downstream. They don't address what's actually destroying the filters." "Imagine you have a screened porch and the screens are rusting. Instead of stopping the rust, you keep wiping down the porch furniture every week. For a while the porch looks fine. But the screens are still corroding. The holes are still getting bigger. You haven't fixed anything. You're just keeping the surface clean." "That's what these drugs are doing. Wiping the surface while the filters rust through. The fatigue, the swelling, the brain fog, the weight loss, the nocturia — that's what happens when the filters get damaged enough that the body can't keep up. The drug doesn't address why the filters are damaged. It just manages the number the doctor watches." She pulled out another printout from the notebook. "And here's the part that explained Walter's slide. And Earl's fatigue. And why people on these medications end up on dialysis anyway." "Your nephrons are under constant attack from two specific toxic molecules. The first is called peroxynitrite. The second is called the hydroxyl radical. They're the most destructive free radicals your body produces when it's under metabolic stress — from high blood pressure, from high blood sugar, from inflammation. They tear holes in the membranes of the tiny filters inside your kidneys, and once a nephron is destroyed it does not grow back. Your body is supposed to neutralize them. But the antioxidants in your bloodstream are too large to reach the inside of the glomerulus — the filtration unit. There's one specific class of small antioxidant molecules that does reach it. They're called anthocyanins." "When anthocyanin levels are high in the bloodstream, the peroxynitrite and hydroxyl radicals get neutralized before they reach the filter. The filters stay intact. eGFR stays stable. The body filters the way it was built to. When anthocyanin levels are low — which they are for almost every American over fifty whose diet doesn't include deeply pigmented plant foods — the radicals run wild. The filters scar. They fail. eGFR drops. Doctor calls it 'progression consistent with stage,' which is medical speak for 'we expect you to keep getting worse so here's a follow-up appointment.' But it's not progression. It's a missing antioxidant. The one antioxidant small enough to reach the place where the damage is happening." "Margaret. Mr. Whitaker. That's not a side effect of CKD. That's the mechanism. That's what's actually destroying the filters while the doctor is watching a number that takes months to show what already happened. Every day for twelve years, Earl has been taking medications that manage the pressure while the antioxidant his nephrons actually need has been missing the entire time. And his doctor is calling it Stage 3a and suggesting an antidepressant." I thought about Earl staring past me at the rocking chairs at Cracker Barrel. For ten months. And his doctor offering him a prescription for depression. I stared at the printouts on the table. At the handwritten notes in the margins. I couldn't speak. Joyce smiled. For the first time in the conversation. "I found something. The mechanism was different from anything else I'd looked at. Everything else was working downstream — managing a number, restricting a food. This one worked upstream — at the damage itself." She turned to another section of the notebook. "I started where I never thought I'd start. A medical journal database at the public library. The keyword was 'anthocyanin glomerular oxidation.' I expected to find nothing. The active compound is called delphinidin-3-sambubioside. It's one of the smallest anthocyanin molecules ever measured. Small enough to cross into the glomerular filtration unit and neutralize peroxynitrite right where it forms. Every other antioxidant you've heard of — vitamin C, vitamin E, CoQ10, glutathione — they're too large to reach the inside of the nephron. They protect blood vessels, they protect cells in general, but they can't get into the filter itself. That's why CKD patients can take antioxidant supplements for years and watch their eGFR keep sliding. Delphinidin-3-sambubioside does reach it. That's the missing piece." She looked at the Bigelow box still sitting at the edge of the table. "And that's why what you bought at Kroger wouldn't do it. Carolyn Pickett made hers in a glass casserole dish. Annette Wadsworth made hers in a tupperware that used to be a different color before the dishwasher got to it. They set them down on the long folding table in the fellowship hall and stepped back and looked at each other and didn't laugh the way they would have ten years ago. They just looked. I watched June straighten her napkin and Carolyn cross her arms and Annette pick a piece of lint off her sleeve that wasn't there. And I thought about the year before, when there had been two identical Jell-O salads and the women had laughed about it and decided it was a sign that they had been friends too long. A woman I had been nodding at for almost a year at my mother's assisted living facility sat down at my table in the visitors' lounge last October. She said: I can't do another Sunday in this room by myself. Is it alright if I sit at your table? I said yes. Two hours later, when she stood up to leave, she had said one sentence to me that has been with me every day since. I am writing this letter because I had been carrying two people quietly for the eighteen months before that Sunday. My eighty-six-year-old mother, in her assisted living room forty minutes from my house. And my sixty-seven-year-old husband, in our living room. That woman gave me back one of them. My name is Joan. I live in a small town outside Buffalo with my husband, Greg. We have been married for thirty-seven years. Greg was a project manager at a manufacturing plant for forty-one years. He retired three years ago. We have one son and one daughter, both in their thirties, both living within an hour of us. I retired four years ago after thirty-two years of doing the office administration for our parish. We were, on paper, supposed to be entering the easiest years of our life. My mother, Rita, is eighty-six. She fell in her own kitchen eighteen months ago. She broke her hip and recovered the way an eighty-six-year-old recovers from a broken hip, which is mostly but not all the way. She has been living at a small assisted living facility called Linden Grove since then. My brother lives in Cleveland and comes when he can. I visit on Sundays. Sometimes Wednesdays, when I can. I bring her a small bag of clementines because she has loved clementines since I was a little girl. She remembers some things and forgets others. She is still my mother and she is mostly herself and the gap between mostly and entirely is the gap I have been quietly grieving for eighteen months. My husband, Greg, is sixty-seven. He has no medical diagnosis I could name for you. He is not on any prescription medications. His doctor — Dr. Anderson, a careful man we have been seeing for twenty-one years — had been mentioning, at Greg's last three annual physicals, that his cholesterol numbers had been creeping. He had been telling Greg that we were getting close to the point where he was going to want to put him on something small. Greg had been telling Dr. Anderson that he wanted six more months to work on it on his own. Dr. Anderson had been giving him six more months. That was the clinical version of where Greg was. The version I had been living with was harder to put into words. It looked like this. It looked like the golf clubs in the corner of the garage, where Greg had set them down after his Saturday morning round eighteen months ago, sitting in exactly the same spot every Saturday morning since. It looked like the truck Greg had washed every other Saturday for forty years, sitting in the driveway with road dust on it for the better part of a year. It looked like Greg sitting in his recliner at three in the afternoon, falling asleep with the newspaper open on his lap, in a way he had never been a man who napped. It looked like our evening walk — a mile and a half around the neighborhood, every night for twenty-six years — shrinking to four blocks and then three blocks and then around the block, with Greg waiting on the porch when I went the rest of the way alone. It looked like Greg, at sixty-seven, declining quietly in our living room at the same time that I was driving to Linden Grove on Sundays to visit my mother declining quietly in hers. I had been telling myself it was retirement. I had been telling myself it was sixty-seven. I had been telling myself it was the year my mother fell. I had been telling myself a lot of things. October last year, on a Sunday afternoon, I was sitting at a small round table in the visitors' lounge at Linden Grove. The lounge is called the Sunshine Room because it has windows on three sides. My mother had been moved to the medical wing that morning. She had a small infection. Nothing serious. They were keeping her on antibiotics for a few days. I was sitting in the Sunshine Room waiting for the nurse to come tell me when I could go back and see her. I was on my third paper cup of bad coffee. I was not in a good way. A woman I had been nodding at in the hallway at Linden Grove for almost a year sat down at the table next to mine. She was about my age. Silver hair, cut short. A canvas tote bag with a paperback book in it. She set the bag down and put her elbows on the table and her face in her hands for a moment. Then she looked up at me and said: I can't do another Sunday by myself in this room. Is it alright if I sit at your table? I said yes. She moved her coffee over. She told me her name was Patricia. She told me she went by Trish. She told me she had been visiting her father at Linden Grove for three years. I told her I had been visiting my mother for eighteen months. We sat at that table for two hours. I am not going to give you the whole conversation. It is the conversation two women in their late fifties or early sixties have when they have been quietly doing the same thing alone for too long and finally find someone else who is also quietly doing it. We talked about our parents. We talked about the gap between mostly and entirely. We talked about the moment you realize your mother is not coming back to where she was. We talked about siblings who are far away. We talked about the way Sunday afternoons in the Sunshine Room are very long. About an hour and a half in, Trish said something offhand about her husband. She said: I am tired in a way that has me worried, because my husband, Ron, is tired the same way. He is sixty-nine. He has been quietly slowing down for years. I cannot afford to be slowing down at the same time he is, because there is no one else for either of these old people. I told her about Greg. I told her about the golf clubs in the garage. I told her about the truck. I told her about the four blocks shrinking to around the block. I told her about the recliner at three in the afternoon. Trish listened. She nodded. When I was finished, she sat with it for a minute. Then she said something I have been thinking about every day since. She said: About two years ago I added one small thing to Ron's mornings. I read for almost a month before I added it. I talked to his doctor and to his pharmacist before I added it. I want to be very careful with you about what I say next, because Ron is one man and you are looking at one man and bodies are different. But Ron has been more himself, for the last two years, than he was for the four years before that. He has been present at our kitchen table. He has been doing the small Saturday things he had stopped doing. He has been a man I recognize again. She paused. I did not give him anything in particular. I added one small additional thing to a long list of things he was already doing. I kept everything else exactly the same. I would not want you to think I am telling you a fireworks story. I am telling you what happened in our house, alongside everything else we did. I asked her what she had added. She said it was a beetroot capsule. She said the brand was called Rosabella. She said she had picked it because the small company that made it cold-pressed the beetroot at low temperatures rather than processing it with heat, and because Ron's doctor had specifically said that how the beetroot was processed mattered for what would make it from the field into the capsule. She said it the way a woman who has been carrying a load alone tells another woman who has been carrying a load alone what she has been doing. She wasn't selling me anything. She was just telling me. The nurse came in about half an hour later to say I could go back and see my mother. I sat with her for an hour. I drove home thinking about Trish. I drove the rest of that week thinking about Trish. By the weekend, I was thinking about what I was going to do. I went home and I started reading. I read for almost three weeks. I am, by temperament, a careful person. I do not add things to my body or to my husband's body without understanding what I am adding. I read about beetroot. I read about the deep crimson pigment in the root. It is called betalain. It is the color that stains your cutting board for three days. It is also, according to a long, patient body of research the cardiovascular community has been quietly building for decades, one of the more potent antioxidants in the food supply. I read about the long, slowly built relationship the careful structure-function research has had with this vegetable. In the context of supporting healthy circulation. Supporting cardiovascular wellness. Supporting the body's own cellular energy. In people whose numbers are already in the range their doctors want them in. None of what I read was a fireworks story. It was the opposite of one. It was a vegetable that has been quietly studied for a long time by careful people who were not making outlandish claims. The language being used in the careful corner of the conversation was the language I had been quietly hoping to find. Supports healthy circulation. Supports cardiovascular wellness. Supports the body's own cellular energy. Not lowers cholesterol. Not fixes anything. Not replaces what Dr. Anderson had been wanting to put Greg on. That was the right shape. I read about the cold-press, too. The chemistry is straightforward. The betalain pigment is heat-sensitive. If you process beetroot the standard way, with heat, you lose some of the compound to the heat. Rosabella cold-presses at low temperatures because they want as much of the compound as possible to make it from the field into the capsule. That is a slower way to make a supplement. It costs them more. At sixty, after watching my mother lose her independence in eighteen months and my husband lose his Saturday rituals over the same eighteen months, I have come to pay close attention to the small decisions companies make when no one is watching. Those decisions tell you everything. The other thing I liked was the simplicity. Two capsules in the morning with a glass of water. I have a mother forty minutes away. I have a husband on the couch. I have a small life I am trying to hold together. I am not interested in a protocol that requires its own shelf. Now I need to tell you the most important part of this letter. Before I added it to anything Greg was already doing, I called our pharmacist. His name is Paul. He is the pharmacist at the small independent pharmacy in our town. I have been filling things there for over twenty years. I called him for a specific reason. Greg is on no prescription medications. He takes a multivitamin and a vitamin D in the winter. I called Paul anyway. I called because I am a careful person and because I wanted somebody who knew what was on Greg's chart to confirm that adding a beetroot capsule to a multivitamin was the right thing to do at his age. Paul pulled up Greg's profile. He confirmed there were no concerns at the dosage on the label. He told me Greg could take it in the morning with his coffee the way the bottle suggested. He told me to call him back if Dr. Anderson ever started Greg on any prescription medication in the future, because the conversation would be different at that point. He told me, before he got off the phone, that he wished more of his patients made the call I had just made. I also called Dr. Anderson's office that week. I told the nurse what I was thinking about adding for Greg. I told her the brand and the dosage. She talked to Dr. Anderson and called me back the next day. She told me Dr. Anderson had said it was a sensible thing to add — antioxidant support, no concerns at the dosage on the label, nothing to interact with anything Greg was taking — and to let him know how Greg was doing at his next appointment. I want to say something now, plainly, to every reader of this letter. If your husband — or your wife, or your father, or your mother, or the person you are caring for, or you yourself — is on any prescription medication, especially anything cardiovascular, please make the call before you add anything new. I called Paul, and I called Dr. Anderson's office, and Greg was on nothing. I would have called twice as fast if Greg had been on a cardiovascular prescription. So should you. The people who know the chart will tell you in two minutes whether the supplement is safe to add, given what is already being taken. The two minutes the call takes is the most important two minutes of your engagement with any supplement you might consider adding. I told Greg that night. I told him about Trish. I told him about the reading. I told him about Paul and Dr. Anderson. I told him I wanted him to try it for me. He looked at the bottle. He looked at me. We have been married thirty-seven years. Da qualche anno seguo un’alimentazione antinfiammatoria che ha totalmente cambiato il mio corpo (in termini sia di tonicità che di gonfiore addominale) insieme al mio amato pilates e al drenaggio. Purtroppo spesso c’è la convinzione che l’alimentazione antinfiammatoria sia qualcosa di molto difficile da seguire o che richieda cibi particolari, quando invece è soprattutto una questione di scelte. La base sono verdura, cereali integrali, spezie e frutta con una quantità non esagerata di proteine. Ne ho parlato a lungo: in passato mangiavo MOLTE più proteine di ora ed ero ossessionata dai cibi proteici. Ho fatto un passo indietro e mi sento molto meglio oltre a essere meno gonfia. Sicuramente le proteine sono importanti, ma non bisogna esagerare (sinceramente penso che ora ci sia un po’ l’ossessione). Personalmente non mangio quasi mai carne rossa e prediligo invece proteine vegetali o pesce. Recentemente ho smesso di mangiare salmone, prediligendo pesci più piccoli come le sardine, visto che il salmone di allevamento non è il massimo (e trovarlo non di allenamento certificato e sicuro è quasi impossibile). E poi non si deve fare tutto perfetto, ma se si segue questa come base, l’infiammazione scende. Dopo aver visto le 10 idee di colazioni proteiche, in questa seconda parte parliamo di come capire quante proteine assumere durante la giornata. ㅤ ㅤ Le proteine sono indispensabili per il mantenimento e la crescita della massa muscolare, ma anche per la regolazione ormonale, la risposta immunitaria e la sazietà. ㅤ Tuttavia, la quantità ottimale non è uguale per tutte: dipende da peso, livello di attività fisica e obiettivo (dimagrimento, mantenimento o aumento della massa muscolare). 🌸 ㅤ 👉 Le linee guida più aggiornate indicano per una donna che si allena regolarmente un apporto compreso tra 1,6 e 2 g di proteine per kg di peso corporeo al giorno. ㅤ 📍 Esempi pratici: – Donna di 60 kg che si allena 3–4 volte a settimana → circa 90–100 g di proteine al giorno – Donna che si allena con maggiore intensità o segue una fase di ricomposizione corporea → fino a 120 g, sempre valutando la dieta complessiva ㅤ 💡 L’aspetto più importante non è solo la quantità totale, ma come le proteine vengono distribuite nei vari pasti: ogni pasto principale dovrebbe includere una fonte proteica, accompagnata da carboidrati complessi e grassi buoni per un equilibrio ottimale. ㅤ Nel carosello di oggi troverai alcune colazioni proteiche con il pane, un alimento che molte donne amano ma spesso evitano pensando che “faccia ingrassare”. ㅤ In realtà, il pane può far parte di una dieta equilibrata e completa: basta abbinarlo a una buona fonte di proteine e grassi per ottenere un pasto saziante, bilanciato e perfetto per chi si allena 🥖✨ ㅤ Nei prossimi caroselli parleremo di come distribuire le proteine nei pasti della giornata, per capire come organizzare colazioni, pranzi e cene in modo semplice e realistico. ㅤ ㅤ Per informazioni sui nostri percorsi nutrizionali o di allenamento, compila il form che torvi nel link in bio! Di quanto testosterone hai davvero bisogno per crescere? Cosa dice la scienza sui dosaggi 🧪 Molti credono che basti “usare” per diventare enormi, altri pensano che l’allenamento faccia il 99% del lavoro. In questo carosello analizziamo i crudi dati di due degli studi più famosi al mondo (1996 e 2001) sugli effetti di dosi crescenti e sovrafisiologiche. Ecco cosa abbiamo imparato: 📉 Tutto è dose-dipendente (Studio 1): Più alto è il dosaggio (fino a 600 mg/settimana testati), maggiore è l’incremento di massa magra (fino a +7,9 kg) e forza. 🏋️‍♂️ L’allenamento è il vero moltiplicatore (Studio 2): Chi ha usato 600 mg senza allenarsi ha guadagnato +3,2 kg di muscoli. Chi ha combinato la stessa dose con i pesi ha quasi raddoppiato i risultati (+6,1 kg), facendo esplodere i carichi su panca e squat. Why do we cling to meat even when we want to go greener? 🥩 Most of us know that plant-based food is healthier and better for the planet, yet many still reach for the steak. A new study from the University of Copenhagen reveals that the barrier isn't just the taste of meat—it is a lack of "meal knowledge." Researchers found that while people recognize ingredients like tofu or chickpeas, they often don't know how to combine them into a satisfying, complete meal. It is like having the screws and planks for a chair but no manual on how to build it. Key findings from the research: - The Meal Gap: Knowing an ingredient is not enough. Familiarity with full plant-based recipes is the biggest predictor of making the switch. - Food Neophobia: In some cultures, a natural fear of "unfamiliar" foods keeps meat at the center of the plate. - Cultural Differences: While both Denmark and Australia are high meat-consumers, the psychological barriers differ based on how much international cuisine people already eat. The study suggests that to change our habits, we don't just need more vegetables—we need to rethink what a "meal" looks like from the ground up. As a doctor, I get asked about protein all the time—and honestly, a lot of what people believe is just flat-out wrong. No Bake Chocolate Tart is for the chocolate lovers.  It’s decadent and delicious, as well as smooth and creamy.  Some key ingredients included avocado, almond milk, unsweetened cocoa powder and sugar free maple syrup.  The crust is a blend of almonds, coconut flake and cocoa powder and it is incredibly tasty. No Bake Chocolate Tart Ingredients: 1 1/3 Cups of raw almonds, unsalted 1/2 Cup of unsweetened coconut flakes 2 Tablespoons of unsweetened cocoa powder 1/3 Cup + 1 tablespoon of sugar free maple syrup or you can use agave syrup 2 Tablespoon of coconut oil, melted Chocolate Avocado Mousse 1 Cup of avocado, about 3 to 4 avocados (240g 8.5 oz) 1/3 Cup of unsweetened almond milk or you can use rice milk 1/3 Cup + 1 Tablespoon of unsweetened cocoa powder 1/3 Cup + 2 tablespoons of sugar free maple syrup or agave 3 Tablespoon of coconut oil, melted Topping: 1/2 Cup 85% dark chocolate bar, shaved or cut into chunks Directions: -In a blender or a food processor, add all the dry ingredients, raw almonds, unsweetened coconut and cocoa powder. Blend for 30 seconds until the almonds are a thick meal. Then add the maple syrup and melted coconut oil. Then blend again until it’s a sticky dough. If it’s too loose, or dry adjust by adding 1 tablespoon of water if necessary then blend again. Add the sticky dough to the pan, 20 cm (8 inches). I used a 9 inch pan and added the crust to the bottom of the pan. If it’s too sticky, you can also place a piece of parchment paper between your fingers and the dough to prevent sticking to your fingers if desired. Press the dough until it covers the entire pan then put in the refrigerator to set. -To make the chocolate mousse, scoop out the ripe avocado flesh and add to the blender along with the sugar free maple syrup, cocoa powder, unsweetened almond milk and melted coconut oil. Blend ingredients well until coconut is combined. Then pour the chocolate mouse into the prepared pie crust. Add shaved chocolate to the top of the pie to decorate then refrigerate for 4 hours or overnight. Najkompletniji pregled neurologa u Specijalističkom centru Dr Vulić – Banjaluka-zakažite pregled pozivom na broj 051 266 690 U Specijalističkom centru Dr Vulić u Banjaluci, pod stručnim nadzorom prof. dr Zorana Vujkovića, dobićete najkompletniji pregled neurologa. Prof. dr Vujković je priznati neurolog sa dugogodišnjim iskustvom u dijagnostici i lečenju bolesti nervnog sistema, a pregled u ovom centru osigurava vrhunski kvalitet i pažljiv pristup svakom pacijentu. **Kako izgleda pregled neurologa?** Pregled neurologa započinje detaljnom anamnezom, gde neurolog postavlja pitanja u vezi sa vašim simptomima, istorijom bolesti, porodičnom istorijom i eventualnim predispozicijama za neurološke poremećaje. Ovaj razgovor je ključan za postavljanje tačne dijagnoze i dalji tok lečenja. Nakon toga, neurolog vrši temeljni neurološki pregled, koji uključuje procenu refleksa, snage mišića, koordinacije, ravnoteže, vida i drugih neuroloških funkcija. Ovaj deo pregleda omogućava lekaru da uoči eventualne poremećaje u funkcionisanju nervnog sistema, kao što su problemi sa moždanim funkcijama, perifernim nervima, mišićima i drugim delovima tela. Nakon osnovnog neurološkog pregleda, ukoliko je potrebno, neurolog može preporučiti dodatne dijagnostičke testove kao što su EEG (elektroencefalogram), EMG (elektromiografija), ili Doppler ultrazvuk krvnih sudova. **Doppler krvnih sudova glave i vrata:** Jedan od ključnih preventivnih pregleda koji se obavljaju u Specijalističkom centru Dr Vulić je Doppler ultrazvuk krvnih sudova glave i vrata. Ovaj test je neinvazivan i koristi zvučne talase za procenu protoka krvi kroz arterije koje snabdevaju mozak. Doppler ultrazvuk je izuzetno važan za rano otkrivanje problema poput suženja ili blokada krvnih sudova (ateroskleroza, tromboza, plikovi), koji mogu dovesti do ozbiljnih neuroloških poremećaja kao što su moždani udar ili TIA (privremeni ishemijski napad). **Zašto je važno raditi Doppler ultrazvuk preventivno?** Doppler ultrazvuk krvnih sudova glave i vrata omogućava pravovremeno otkrivanje potencijalnih problema u krvotoku koji mogu uzrokovati ozbiljne posledice. Mnogi pacijenti nemaju nikakve simptome sve dok ne dođe do ozbiljnog poremećaja. Preporučuje se svim osobama, naročito onima starijim od 50 godina, sa visokim krvnim pritiskom, dijabetesom, povišenim holesterolom, pušačima, kao i onima sa porodičnom istorijom moždanih udara i srčanih oboljenja, da redovno rade ovaj preventivni pregled. **Zakažite pregled bez čekanja!** Ne čekajte da simptomi postanu ozbiljni. Zakažite pregled u Specijalističkom centru Dr Vulić i osigurajte zdravlje svog nervnog sistema. Pozovite nas odmah na broj 051 266 690 i rezervišite termin bez čekanja. Cuoci i 4 topinambur a vapore finché sono morbidi. Pela e frulla con un filo d’olio e sale, ottenendo una crema liscia. 2. In un tegame fai un soffritto con olio e scalogno tritato. In un pentolino scalda un cucchiaio di olio con rosmarino e aglio per ottenere un olio aromatizzato. 7.     Impiatta la fregola cremosa, aggiungi le chips croccanti e qualche goccia di olio profumato. #chefellen #guthealth #gutdriven #seedcrackers #healthieralternatives ✨Savory Seed Crackers 🌱⅓ cup chia seeds 🌱⅓ cup whole flax seeds 🌱⅓ cup sunflower seeds 🌱⅔ cup pumpkin seeds 🌱¼ cup ground flaxseed 🌱2 heaping tablespoons brown rice flour 🌱½ teaspoon baking powder 🌱¼ teaspoon xanthan or guar gum 🌱Garlic powder, to taste 🌱Onion powder, to taste 🌱Sea salt, to taste 🌱2 tablespoons refined coconut oil, melted 🌱⅓ cup warm water, plus more as needed 🌱Optional: dried oregano, finely chopped fresh rosemary, or dried basil Preheat oven to 325°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. For a cracker that holds together particularly well, lightly pulse the pumpkin and sunflower seeds in a food processor just a few times. You want them roughly broken up, not ground into flour. In a large bowl, combine the chia, flax, sunflower, and pumpkin seeds, ground flaxseed, brown rice flour, baking powder, xanthan or guar gum, and seasonings. Stir in the melted coconut oil and ⅓ cup warm water. Mix thoroughly. Allow the mixture to rest for 15 minutes so the chia and flax can absorb the water and create a natural gel. Check the consistency. The mixture should be thick, slightly sticky, and hold together when pressed. If it seems dry or crumbly, add additional warm water 1 tablespoon at a time. Transfer the mixture to the prepared baking sheet. Place another sheet of parchment on top and roll or press evenly to approximately ⅛-inch thick. Remove the top parchment and score into desired cracker shapes. Bake for approximately 25–30 minutes, or until the cracker sheet feels set and the edges are beginning to crisp. Carefully separate or flip the crackers and return them to the oven for another 10–15 minutes, until dry and crisp. They will become even crisper as they cool. Note: Don’t rush the 15-minute rest. That little bit of time lets the chia and flax create the “glue” that keeps a seed-heavy cracker from falling apart. 0:00 / 0:33 INSTAGRAM.COM Chef Ellen Voir le profil Instagram ​

Daug romantikos, šiltų vasariškų vakarų nuostabioje saloje ir nemažai intriguojančių išgyvenimų – tai puikus derinys nepaprastai skaniam romanui, kurio negalėsite užversti iki paties paskutinio puslapio! Svajones apie tolimus fjordus tenka pamiršti, nes santaupų užtenka tik sodo sklypeliui su miniatiūriniu nameliu Bulholmene – turistų pamėgtame spalvingame Stokholmo archipelage. Svajingoji vietos idilė išsisklaido, kai po tradicinės vasaros saulėgrįžos šventės saloje randama negyva jauna moteris, o Silos gyvenimas pasisuka visiškai nauja linkme. I turned seventy last spring. My cardiovascular bloodwork has been in the ranges my doctor wants it in for twenty-three years, and I have been doing the small careful things to keep it there. I am seventy years old. My name is Eleanor. I have lived in the same small town in central Connecticut for forty-seven years. My husband, John, passed nine years ago — quietly, from a long illness — and I have been here in the house we bought together since 1979, doing the small daily work of being a widow in her seventies who is choosing, as much as she can, to live well. I have one daughter, Karen, who lives an hour from me in Hartford. I have two grandchildren in their twenties. I have a small circle of close friends I have known for thirty and forty years. I worked as a paralegal at the same small law firm in our town from 1981 until I retired at sixty-three. I have been retired for seven years and I have used those seven years carefully. I tell you all of this because the story I want to tell you is not a dramatic story. It is the story of a woman who has been paying patient, quiet attention to her cardiovascular wellness for twenty-three years, and who added one small thing to her mornings a little over a year ago that she wanted to mention to other women like her. I want to start with what I have been doing for the last twenty-three years, because the rest of this letter does not make sense without it. When I was forty-seven, my mother died. She was sixty-eight. She had a heart event in October and a second one in December and she was gone by February. My mother had spent most of her life, by her own admission, not paying very much attention to her cardiovascular wellness. She had eaten the way women of her generation ate, smoked from her twenties to her fifties, walked when she needed to and not when she didn't, and the cardiovascular medications she had been put on in her early sixties had been a too-late addition to a body that had been telling her things she had not been listening to. I sat with all of that for a long time after she died. When I was forty-seven and a half, I went to my own doctor and asked her, plainly, what a woman in her late forties could start doing to make sure she did not have my mother's last few months at sixty-eight.

Dievčatko, ktoré sa ma vždy pýtalo: „Dedko, ešte jednu rozprávku pred spaním.“ Dievčatko, ktoré ma objímalo okolo krku a hovorilo: „Dedko, ešte jedno objatie.“ ❤️ A ako mnoho starých rodičov, aj ja som mal pre ňu obrovskú slabosť. Príliš som ju rozmaznával. Pizza 🍕 Hranolky 🍟 Sladké nápoje 🥤 Sušienky po škole. Malé maškrty cez víkendy. Zakaždým, keď sa usmiala, mal som pocit, že robím niečo dobré. Tak som si opakoval: „Je to len dieťa.“ „Zaslúži si užívať si.“ „Časom sa to zmení.“ Ale postupne som si začal všímať malé zmeny. Sofia mala menej energie. Bola pokojnejšia. Až jedného popoludnia… sa všetko zmenilo. Išli sme po schodoch v mojom dome. V polovici cesty sa zastavila. Chytila sa zábradlia, pozrela dole a ticho mi povedala: „Dedko… som unavená.“ Tá veta vo mne zostala. Nie preto, že by nemohla pokračovať… ale preto, že som si zrazu uvedomil jednu vec: Pomýlil som si lásku s tým, že jej stále dávam malé odmeny. Dal som jej veľa šťastných chvíľ, ale možno nie dosť zdravých návykov. Dal som jej veľa lásky, ale nie dosť rovnováhy. A jej malé telo mi to začínalo ukazovať. Nikdy nešlo iba o vzhľad. Ale mal som jednu veľmi jasnú vec: Nechcel som, aby Sofia cítila hanbu. Nechcel som prísne diéty. Nechcel som, aby pohyb vyzeral ako trest. A nikdy som nechcel, aby sa pozerala do zrkadla so smútkom. Chcel som len, aby sa opäť cítila: silnejšia, aktívnejšia, a šťastná taká, aká je. ❤️ Potom sme sa rozhodli začať malými zmenami. Najdôležitejšie sú malé každodenné návyky: vyvážená strava, viac pohybu, dostatok kvalitného spánku a veľa emocionálnej podpory.“ Táto veta zmenila môj pohľad na všetko. Keď sme sa vrátili domov, dal som si sľub: Tentoraz ju nebudem iba rozmaznávať. Budem ju sprevádzať. Bez tlaku. Bez hádok. Bez výčitiek. Len s trpezlivosťou, láskou a vytrvalosťou. Tak sme začali postupne: 💧 Viac vody. 🥗 Vyváženejšie jedlá. 🍎 Menej automatického maškrtenia. 🏡 Viac domácich jedál. 🚶 Krátke prechádzky po večeri. 🌙 Pravidelnejší čas spánku. A jedno jediné pravidlo: „Dnes musíme urobiť iba jedno dobré rozhodnutie.“ Na začiatku sa nič nezdalo výnimočné. Ale po niekoľkých týždňoch sme začali vidieť malé zmeny: ✔ Pýtala si menej sladkostí ✔ Mala viac energie ✔ Pohybovala sa ľahšie ✔ Cítila sa pohodlnejšie vo svojom oblečení ✔ Častejšie sa usmievala Po určitom čase sme nevideli iba fyzické zmeny. Najkrajšie bolo vidieť, ako sa jej vracia sebavedomie. Jedného popoludnia Sofia pribehla ku mne v záhrade s obrovským úsmevom a veľmi silno ma objala. 🤗 A tentoraz… som ju dokázal opäť zdvihnúť bez toho, aby som cítil, že je to pre mňa náročné. Ten moment ma naučil niečo dôležité: Nikdy nešlo iba o číslo na váhe. Išlo o to dať mojej vnučke príležitosť vyrastať s pocitom, že je silná, sebavedomá, šťastná a hlboko milovaná. La meg dele innholdet i kortversjon🥰 Det spørsmålet eg oftast får, er kva oppskrifter boka inneholder - og det ligger litt i tittelen: dette er ei middagsbok! Middagsbok med fokus på sunne, raske og enkle kvardagsmiddager + litt ekstra 🙂 Det eg personlig liker aller best er kapittelinndelinga, der lesaren kan finne ein fristande oppskrift i det kapittelet som passer best: → Middagar på maks 20 minutt → Middagar ein kan lage klar kvelden før → Alt-i-eitt midddagar → Restemiddagar → Middagar for ein person → Middagar med maks 6 ingredienser → Helgemiddagar → Tilbehørtips til middagen Genialt, eller kva? Det synes vertfall eg! Eg vil og få fram at boka har stor variasjon i oppskriftene: alt fra kjøtt, fisk, kylling og vegetar i ulike oppskrifter som suppe, gryte, grateng, salater, tallerkenretter m.m🥙 Boka inneholder 80 oppskrifter, der over halvparten (ca 45 av dei) ikkje er delt på bloggen tidligare. Av desse oppskriftene har eg satt sammen 10 forskjellige vekemenyer MED tilhøyrande handleliste også🤩👏🏻 I tillegg vil eg få fram at ein trenger ikkje noken spesialingredienser, kun vanlige ingredienser fra dagligvarebutikken - og ikkje minst at alle oppskriftene er merka med symbol som viser om oppskrifta er glutenfri/melkefri/vegetarisk💛 Må og nevne at det her er meir enn berre ei kokebok, med mange ulike tekster med tips & råd til korleis ein skal ta bedre valg når det kjem til matvalg, planlegging, sparing av penger, unngå matsvinn og bruke opp matrestene👏🏻 Så, kort fortalt er dette boka for oss som sliter med tidsklemma, som syns middagsmat er ei utfordring, og for oss som treng inspirasjon til å løfte middagen til nye høgder på ein enkel måte! ad_text: Tag din datter i hånden og træd ind i en weekend fyldt med nærvær, ro og fælles oplevelser på bilfri & naturskønne Bjørnø. Læs meget mere om mor & datter retreatet og få tilsendt en gratis prøvetime på Sansebaseret Yoga igennem linket. Jeg glæder mig helt vildt til at møde dig. Bli med på en uforglemmelig reise for kropp, sinn og sjel. Midt i den mørke og kalde vinteren i Norge inviteres du med på en yoga ferie-retreat i Goa – som kombinerer yoga, sol, varme, strand & hav , rom for hvile og velvære , og Indisk kultur fellesskap. Dette er en reise for å varme kroppen, roe sinnet og fylle på med lys, varme og NY ENERGI, i idylliske omgivelser ved havet i Mandrem, Nord-Goa. Om retreatet Retreatet holdes på Nalanda Retreat i Nord-Goa, et veletablert og anerkjent yogasenter rett ved stranden. Her skaper vi en trygg, rolig og inkluderende ramme rundt dagene – hvor yoga, strand & hav -og indisk tradisjon smelter sammen. Retreatet starter lørdag 20. februar (morgen) og avsluttes lørdag 27. februar (kveld).  Avreise fra Norge fredag 19. februar, og retur søndag 28 februar-27 Ønsker du et lengre opphold i Goa, kan du gjerne komme noen dager før eller bli litt lenger etter retreatet. Arrangøren kan være behjelpelig med overnatting og praktisk planlegging, enten i Goa eller andre destinasjoner i India. Om du ønsker kan du selvsagt kombinere yogaretreatet med litt reising i India, enten før eller etter oppholdet i Goa ! ⸻ Yoga & daglig rytme Yogaen vil være variert og tilgjengelig – fra litt mer aktiv morgenyoga til rolig, nærende og restorativ praksis. Det vil være flere yogatimer daglig gjennom 8 dager , tilpasset gruppen og energien i retreatet. Dagene har en naturlig og behagelig rytme: – Yoga og morgenpraksis – Deilig frokost ved stranden, i retreatets åpne lounge – Tid til strandliv, hvile og egentid – Enkelte dager felles utflukter – Rolig samling eller myk yoga på ettermiddag – Felles middag ved stranden På kvelden er det også mulighet for meditasjon, chanting og beachfire ved stranden. Retreatet åpnes og avsluttes med en tradisjonell pooja-seremoni, ledet av en lokal hindu. Seremonien brukes til å samle gruppen, skape felles fokus og markere starten og avslutningen på oppholdet på en jordnær og meningsfull måte. Du trenger absolutt ingen tidligere erfaring med yoga. Dette retreatet passer for alle. ⸻ Måltider Måltidene er en viktig del av retreatopplevelsen og støtter rytmen gjennom dagen. Maten på Nalanda Retreat er vegetarisk, med innslag av fisk, og tilberedt med fokus på ferske, lokale og sesongbaserte råvarer. Frokost og middag nytes i retreatets åpne restaurant ved stranden og gir rom for både ro, samtale og fellesskap. ⸻ Opplevelser & fellesskap I tillegg til yoga og egentid inngår felles opplevelser og utflukter i retreatprogrammet. Eksempler på opplevelser kan være: – Sunrise dolphin boat trip – Friday Night Market – Besøk i Old Goa – Felles tempelbesøk *Disse opplevelsene betales separat. ⸻ Spa & velvære Nalanda Retreat har eget spa med ayurvedisk helsekonsultasjon, massasje og holistiske behandlinger. For deg som ønsker ekstra pleie, fordypning og velvære under oppholdet. ⸻ Hva retreatet inkluderer Prisen inkluderer: – 8 dager retreat / 7 overnattinger – Daglig frokostbuffet og middagsbuffet – All yoga aktivitet gjennom 8 dager – Tradisjonell Indisk åpnings- og avslutnings-pooja – Privat yoga-shala eksklusivt for vår gruppe - Yoga matte+alt annet utstyr til yoga – Vann, chai samt sitron- og ingefærte tilgjengelig hele dagen – Sengetøy, håndklær og daglig housekeeping – Full tilgang til to svømmebassenger, relaxation areas og hager – Privat strand med solsenger – WiFi og aircondition – Resepsjon- og concierge-service – Beachfire og felles ritualer ⸻ Rom & priser per person /  Investering i deg selv ♥️ Prisene gjelder for hele retreatopplevelsen – 8 dager / 7 netter 🌿 HILLSIDE (ca. 200 meter fra stranden) Classic Room – Double: €810 – Single: €1.030 Heritage Room – Double: €880 – Single: €1.160 🌊 BEACHSIDE (0–20 meter fra stranden) Classic Room – Double: €900 – Single: €1.200 Heritage Room – Double: €965 – Single: €1.330 🛏️ Dobbeltrom – praktisk informasjon For deltakere som velger dobbeltrom, vil romfordelingen gjøres ved ankomst til retreatet. Vill du förgylla sommaren med en helg som verkligen gör avtryck? ❤️ Den 8-9 augusti håller jag yogaretreat på Smögens Hafvsbad — ett av Bohusläns vackraste hotell, med havet precis utanför. Det här är inte ett vanligt retreat. Det är två dagar av fördjupning, rörelse och inspiration för dig som vill ta din yogapraktik vidare och lämna med nya verktyg och en energi som håller långt efter helgen är slut. ad_text: En musikalisk helkväll i samarbete med Hållandsgården. I orostider när många känner rädsla och hjälplöshet kan det egna skapandet, mötet med naturen och gemenskap med andra människor ge oss perspektiv, kraft och inspiration att se framåt. Det är mot den fonden som föreställningen Förnimmelser har vuxit fram och tagit form. Genom poesi, musik och sång vill vi lyfta både egna och några av samtidens mångfacetterade frågor och känslor för att på så sätt få syn på dem. I föreställningen flätas orden samman med musiken till en helhet som bär på en önskan att lyfta hoppet och stärka motståndskraften så att vi tillsammans kan föreställa oss och forma en ljusare framtid. Marianne Folkedotter är berättare, poet och låtskrivare som i en rad uppmärksammade och uppskattade berättarföreställningar visat sin förmåga att med orden upplysa, entusiasmera och förundra en stor publik i och utanför Västerbotten. 2022 debuterade hon med diktsamlingen ”En skog som går omkring bland husen” som sedan iscensattes med musik av och med Rickard N Jokela. Rickard N Jokela är basist och kompositör med influenser från jazz, indisk raga och modern konstmusik. Efter resor i bland annat Japan, Indien och Schweiz har han utvecklat ett eget förhållande till improvisation och komposition med just solospel i fokus. Konserten arrangeras i samarbete med Hållandsgården som erbjuder vegetarisk buffé innan föreställningen. Samt med ekonomiskt stöd från Jämtkraft, Swedbanks Ägarstiftelse Jämtlands Län och Åre kommun. Ingredienser: • 500 g blandfärs • 1 msk matolja till stekning • ½ gul lök • 2 morötter • 3-4 stora vitlöksklyftor • 3 msk tomatpuré • 2 msk ketchup i bolognesen (valfritt) • 1 burk (400 g) krossade tomater • 2 dl vispgrädde • 1,5 msk torkad timjan • ca 0.5 tsk salt • 30 drag svartpeppar • 2 Knorr Fond du Chef Beef • 0,5 msk japansk soja • ca 2 dl vatten Gör så här: Hetta upp lite matolja i en stekpanna eller gryta och bryn blandfärsen på hög värme så att den får ordentligt med färg. Krydda med salt och svartpeppar. Tillsätt hackad gul lök och morot. Sänk värmen och låt det mjukna i 5–10 minuter, gärna under lock. Tillsätt de rivna vitlöksklyftorna och fräs försiktigt på låg värme utan att vitlöken tar färg. Tillsätt mer olja om det behövs. Rör ner tomatpurén och låt den fräsa med några minuter. Tillsätt krossade tomater, vatten och timjan. Rör om ordentligt. Tillsätt Knorr Fond du Chef Beef och rör om. Häll i grädden och tillsätt ketchup och japansk soja. Rör om och låt grädden försiktigt koka ner i ca 10 min. Smaka av och justera med salt och svartpeppar vid behov. Servera med pasta. Testa Fond du Chef själv! 0:00 / 0:31 ​

Sätt ugnen på 225 grader varmluft. 2. Skär aubergine och zucchini i ca 2 cm tjocka halvmånar. Blanda med salt i en bunke och låt stå i rumstemperatur i ca 20–30 minuter. 3. Hetta upp en stekpanna på medelhög värme. 4. Skär vitlöken i tunna skivor och dela chilin på längden. Stek tillsammans med olivolja. När vitlöken fått lite färg, tillsätt salt och basilika. Efter 1–2 minuter, häll i Mutti Polpa och lite vatten. Låt sjuda på medelvärme. 5. När grönsakerna har rimmas klart, krama ur vätskan med en ren kökshandduk. Ringla över olivolja och lägg ut grönsakerna på bakplåtspapper. Försök att inte lägga dem för mycket på varandra. Rosta i ugnen i ca 30 minuter. Efter ca 15 minuter, eller när de fått färg, ta ut plåten och rör om. Rosta sedan vidare tills grönsakerna fått ordentligt med färg. 6. Låt tomatsåsen sjuda utan att koka ner för mycket. Den ska fortfarande vara relativt lös, men ha mycket smak och bra intensitet – tillsammans med de ugnsrostade grönsakerna är det som ger lasagnen mycket av dess karaktär. 7. Vispa ihop vispgrädde och crème fraîche tills såsen är homogen. 8. Riv parmesanen och skär mozzarellan i ca 1 cm tjocka bitar. 9. Bygg ihop lasagnen. Börja med ett tunt lager vit sås som precis täcker botten, så att lasagneplattorna inte fastnar. Fortsätt sedan i följande ordning och upprepa tills lasagnen är klar (ca 4 lager): lasagneplattor, tomatsås, vit sås, grönsaker och parmesan. I mitten av lasagnen lägger du även i en näve basilikablad. Avsluta med mozzarella och ringla över lite olivolja för en gratinerad och ostig yta. 10. Täck lasagnen med aluminiumfolie och grädda i 225 grader varmluft i ca 25 minuter. 🍑 GLUTEO PIATTO E PIENO DI BUCHETTI: ECCO PERCHÉ SQUAT E AFFONDI NON BASTANO Fai squat e affondi tre volte a settimana… e l’unica cosa che progredisce è la frustrazione quando ti specchi di profilo. 😩 Non è colpa del tuo impegno – è colpa di due meccanismi anatomici che nessuno ti ha mai spiegato. 🧬 Nella tua gamba c’è una vena importantissima: la vena grande safena. Sale dal piede, attraversa la coscia e all’inguine si collega alla vena femorale per portare il sangue al cuore. ❤️ Quel punto preciso si chiama crosse safeno-femorale – ed è qui che tutto si blocca. Quando fai uno squat profondo o un affondo statico, chiudi esattamente quel punto. ⚠️ I liquidi non risalgono, il gluteo non viene ossigenato correttamente… e si formano i buchetti. 🍊 In più, l’elettromiografia dimostra che squat e affondi attivano molto di più il quadricipite rispetto al gluteo – ecco perché rimane piatto. ❌ Nel Metodo CB Coaching applichiamo tre principi diversi: ✨ Esercizi in catena cinetica aperta che attivano il gluteo senza chiudere la crosse safeno-femorale. ✨ Esercizi di isolamento per tutti i fasci del gluteo – tonicità senza ingrossare le cosce. ✨ Routine mirate per ossigenare la zona e eliminare i buchetti davvero. 🌿 Con questi tre principi oltre 6.000 donne hanno ritrovato un gluteo alto, sodo e senza buchetti. 🧡 0:00 / 1:34 ​

🍑BANANA ROLLS SOTTO IL GLUTEO: ECCO PERCHÉ NON SPARISCONO MAI 👇🏻 Ti alleni, ti impegni, carichi sullo squat… ma quei rotolini sotto al gluteo sono ancora lì. 😤 Non è colpa tua – è che stai attaccando il problema nel modo sbagliato. I banana rolls hanno 3 cause precise: mancanza di rassodamento dei fasci profondi del grande gluteo, lombare poco mobile o piatta e stasi venosa da circolazione rallentata. 🆘 Aggiungere più esercizi a caso o più carico non risolve nulla. L’unico risultato che ottieni è gambe più gonfie e un gluteo che si attiva sempre meno. ❌ E nel tempo, la zona sotto-gluteo cede e perde tono definitivamente. ⚠️ La soluzione è allenarsi – ma nel modo giusto, seguendo 3 step precisi. ✅ 1️⃣ Esercizi mirati per i fasci bassi del gluteo come reverse hyper, step up controllato e slanci per definire i dettagli. 🍑 2️⃣ Recupero fisiologico della lombare tramite mobilità mirata ed esercizi gluteo-specifici che stimolano l’allungamento. 🌿 3️⃣ Routine di scarico venoso attive – anche solo 5/10 minuti al giorno per sbloccare le pompe venose dal piede al gluteo e liberare i ristagni. 💧 Sono esattamente questi 3 step che hanno aiutato oltre 6.000 donne a far sparire i banana rolls, nonostante anni di allenamenti sbagliati. 🧡 0:00 / 1:16 ​

They registered my brother legally blind last spring. The doctor said the pressure in his blood vessels did it. He's 58. I'm 56. We have the same numbers. My brother and I have the same blood. Same father. Our dad died of heart disease. His father went the same way. Everyone in my family, both sides, ends up on blood pressure pills. I used to check my own number every morning at the kitchen table. I'd see 145 over 92 and tell myself it was fine. Not great. But fine. My doctor wanted to see me again in three months. If it wasn't better, she said, we would talk about medication. For years I told myself I would be the one who beat it. I was the careful one. I watched what I ate. Then last March, my brother's body started coming apart. One piece at a time. It started with his eyes. He kept rubbing them at dinner, saying the edges were going gray. Six weeks later they told him the pressure had blown out the vessels in his retinas. Legally blind. At 58. Then his kidneys. They said he was close to needing dialysis. Three mornings a week, hooked to a machine, his whole calendar built around it. Then his heart. Enlarged. Working too hard for too long. Then his legs. The veins gave out and his ankles swelled like he was carrying water in them. And then the part nobody warned us about. His mind. He would lose the word he was reaching for halfway through a sentence. He started writing things on the back of his hand so he would not forget them. I started driving him to his appointments. Me. Driving my big brother around like he was the kid. I went home from that first appointment and swore it would not be me. So I tried everything. The low-sodium diet my wife found. Everything tasted like cardboard. I dropped maybe five points. I cut out beer for three months. Went from 148 to 143. Three months of saying no, for five points. I joined the gym in January. Made it six weeks before work blew up. The number barely moved anyway. I spent a hundred and fifty dollars on supplements from the health food store. Fish oil. CoQ10. Took them every day for three months. Could not tell you if they did one thing. I even tried hibiscus. The grocery-store tea bags first. Then the "blood pressure" tea blend off the shelf. Then a cranberry-hibiscus drink, and a bottle of hibiscus capsules off Amazon. Nothing. One night I sat on the edge of the bed and listened to my own heart thump in the dark. And I thought the thing I had been trying not to think. Maybe genetics already made the call. Maybe there was nothing I could do. Then one night it came for me. I woke up in the dark with my face pounding. That thick pressure behind the eyes, like the worst part of the flu. My heart was going so hard I could hear it in the pillow. I lay there certain this was how it started for him. I thought about his eyes. His kidneys. The words he cannot find anymore. And I was lying in the same bed, in the same body, still guessing. I had been guessing for months. At my brother's next appointment, I did not sit in the corner like I always did. I waited until the nurse took him back for his bloodwork. Then I stopped his specialist in the hallway. "I have what he has," I said. "Same numbers. Same family." My voice cracked. I had not planned for that. "Is this where I'm headed?" She looked at me for a second. Then she walked me over to the empty chairs in the waiting room and sat down. "Most people think high blood pressure is about salt," she said. "It's really about whether your blood vessels can still open, and whether the lining inside them is holding up." She told me that the inside of every vessel has a thin lining, and that lining is what tells the walls to relax and widen, so blood moves through without strain. "As you get older, and as the pressure climbs, that lining takes a beating," she said. "Years of pressure and the wear we call oxidative stress chew it up. The vessels stiffen. They stop being able to open all the way." She held up her hand and pinched two fingers almost shut. "Picture a garden hose that's gone stiff and narrow with age. Same water. Nowhere to go. So the pressure climbs." I asked what that had to do with my brother's eyes. She got quiet. "The smallest vessels go first. The eyes. The kidneys. The brain. It isn't five separate diseases. It's the same pressure and the same wear, finding the weakest pipes." Everything I had watched happen to him lined up in a single row. "So why didn't the diet work?" I asked. "Because food alone barely moves the needle once you're at your stage. You needed something that actually protects that lining and helps the vessels stay relaxed. And you were probably drinking a broken version of it." She told me the plants with the deepest red and purple color are loaded with compounds called anthocyanins and polyphenols, and that those are some of the strongest things we know of for defending the vessel lining and helping it keep its tone. Hibiscus, she said, is one of the richest sources there is. "There are studies on hibiscus," she said. "In the better ones, drinking it daily brought blood pressure down around eight to ten points." "Wait," I said. "I tried hibiscus. Four different kinds. It did nothing." She almost laughed. "Of course it did nothing." "Here's what nobody tells you," she said. "Almost every hibiscus product on the shelf is dust and flavoring. Old crop, cut with filler, sometimes nothing but the color and the tartness. Then I asked the question I was almost ashamed of. "How do I know it's not just in my head?" "Because the number comes down over weeks, on your own monitor, in your own kitchen. That part isn't a feeling. It's a reading." I told her about a man I had read about who trusted a supplement for his heart and died anyway. She nodded slowly. "That's exactly why you never do this instead of your doctor. You do it with your doctor. You track the number. If it doesn't move, you'll know fast." "And my family?" I said. "The genetics?" "Genetics loads the gun. The pressure pulls the trigger. Your brother is proof of what the pressure does. He is not proof that you can't lower yours." I asked her the last thing on my mind. "So what do I actually buy?" "I'm not going to hand you a brand," she said. "I'll tell you what has to be true. You go find it." She counted them on her fingers. "Whole flower, not dust or flavoring, grown high so the anthocyanins run deep. Dried gently so the actives survive. Most wouldn't even say where the flower came from. The ones that did wouldn't show a test. After two weeks I still hadn't found one I trusted. I was starting to think she'd sent me looking for something that didn't exist. That Saturday I took my grandson to his soccer game. I was on the sideline with the other grandparents, half watching, when one of the younger dads asked how I was doing. I don't know why I said it. It just came out. "Honestly? Chasing my own blood pressure. My doctor told me to find a whole-flower hibiscus, grown high, with a lab test on it. I've looked everywhere. It's all junk." The man next to me turned around. Older than me. Maybe seventy. "Whole flower? Grown up high?" "Yeah." "That's the one I drink. PiPi Tea. The only one I found that's hand-picked whole flowers and posts the lab results for the batch." He shrugged like it was nothing. "My doctor had me a month from pills. Numbers have been good for a year now." I just looked at him. Two weeks of reading labels, and the answer was sitting in a folding chair on a soccer field. That night I pulled it up. PiPi Tea. Organic whole-flower hibiscus, grown high in the mountains, hand-picked. Everything she had told me to look for was right there. Whole flower, not dust. High-altitude grown so the color and the anthocyanins run deep. And the Certificate of Analysis, batch dated, showing every contaminant test they ran and what came back clean.
